FrMS88-de4655-d1e111.summary: Poses the thirteenth question — whether any transcendental notion is more common than being — and identifies two sources of difficulty: distribution ('positive' is distributed over being and over truth and goodness, so is more common) and numeration (we count the notions of good, true, and being as three notions, so 'notion' is common to them). Announces four conclusions.
claims: Objection: 'positive' and 'notion' seem more common than being.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e140.summary: First conclusion: although no first-intention notion is more common than being, some second-intention notion is. 'Pure perfection' is said of being and truth by the same name and definition (in anything it is better to be it than not); being and truth are formally distinct and each has a formal notion, so 'formal notion' is said of both; and 'universal' is said of both by the same notion.
claims: No first-intention notion is more common than being.
Second intentions such as 'pure perfection', 'formal notion', and 'universal' are more common than being.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e173.summary: Second conclusion: among transcendental respects something is more common than being, since distinction is common to all distinct items and order to all ordered items, and being, true, and good are distinct and ordered.
claims: Distinction and order are more common than being.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e186.summary: Third conclusion: among aptitudes something is more common than being, namely intelligibility and volibility, said of being and of other notions.
claims: Intelligibility and volibility are more common than being.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e194.summary: Fourth conclusion: among privatives something is more common than being, namely unity, said of being and of its attributes, each of which is one (truth is one, goodness is one). Then introduces four objections, the first beginning: every more common notion is prior.
claims: Unity, a privation, is more common than being.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e207.summary: Completes the first objection: every more common notion is prior, but second intentions are not prior to being.
claims: Objection: second intentions are not prior to being, so not more common.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e214.summary: Second objection: whatever is divided by some items is more common than each; being is divided into absolute and respective, while distinction and order are neither absolute nor respective, so none of them is more common than being.
claims: Objection: being, divided into absolute and respective, is more common than distinction and order.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e223.summary: Third objection: no adequate attribute exceeds its subject; true and good are adequate attributes of being.
claims: Objection: adequate attributes cannot exceed being.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e230.summary: Fourth objection: what prescinds from and is formally distinct from something is one as such; goodness is so distinct from being, so it is one; since unity is said of being, a proper attribute would be more common than being.
claims: Objection: unity would be a proper attribute more common than its subject.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e246.summary: Reply to the first: more common items are prior only among quidditative commons; otherwise the more common may be posterior, as genus, a second intention, is more common than animal but not prior.
claims: Greater commonness implies priority only among quidditative commons.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e256.summary: Reply to the second: animal (not animality) is divided into rational and irrational; likewise being taken in its commonness denominatively is divided into absolute and respective, while entity or the prescinded formal notion of being is narrower and not so divided. Reply to the others: the aptitudes and unity are adequate attributes not of prescinded entity but of being taken simply.
claims: Being taken denominatively is divided; prescinded entity is narrower and not divided.
Unity and the aptitudes are attributes of being taken simply, not of prescinded entity.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e278.summary: Raises a doubt: how is being taken in its full latitude? Not as the prescinded notion of being, which is not concrete nor said of all; not as the substrates, which lack unity (divinity and humanity share no notion once being is prescinded); nor as an aggregate, since a part of an aggregate is never predicated in quid of the whole.
claims: Objection: being in its full latitude cannot be the prescinded notion, the substrates, or an aggregate.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e300.summary: Reply: being supposits for the substrates, though not as if the notion of entity were not understood with them as primary; being is predicated in relation to entity, as 'white' supposits for subjects in relation to whiteness.
claims: 'Being' supposits for substrates in relation to entity, as 'white' for subjects in relation to whiteness.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e311.summary: Raises a further doubt: in essentially ordered things, wherever the posterior is the prior is (wherever white, there whiteness); the notion of entity is prior to being, so wherever being is found, entity is. Also, a formal effect seems no wider than its form, and being is the formal effect of entity.
claims: Objection: entity must be found and predicated wherever being is.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e327.summary: Adds: wherever being is found, entity is found.

FrMS88-de4655-d1e332.summary: Reply: although in essentially ordered things the prior is wherever the posterior is, the prior is not predicated of all of which the posterior is predicated — wood is called white but not whiteness. So where being is, entity is, but being is predicated of some things of which entity is not; likewise for the formal effect.
claims: The prior is present wherever the posterior is but not predicated of all of which the posterior is predicated.

FrMS88-de4655.summary: The thirteenth question of the prologue asks whether there is any transcendental notion more common than being. Two considerations prompt it: 'positive' is distributed over being and over other notions such as truth and goodness, and we number the notions of being, true, and good as 'three notions'. Meyronnes answers with four conclusions: although no first-intention notion is more common than being, some are more common than being among second intentions (e.g. 'pure perfection', 'formal notion', 'universal', said of being and truth by the same definition), transcendental respects (distinction, order), aptitudes (intelligibility, volibility), and privations (unity, which is said of being and of its attributes). He answers objections: more common items need be prior only among quidditative commons (genus, a second intention, is more common than animal but not prior); being taken denominatively in its full latitude is divided into absolute and respective, while the prescinded notion of entity is narrower and not so divided; and unity and the aptitudes are attributes of being taken simply, not of prescinded entity. He explains that 'being' in its full latitude supposits for its substrates, though in relation to entity, as 'white' supposits for subjects in relation to whiteness; and although wherever being is found entity is found, entity is not predicated of everything of which being is predicated.
claims: No first-intention notion is more common than being.
Some second intentions, transcendental respects, aptitudes, and privations are more common than being.
Being taken denominatively is divided into absolute and respective, while prescinded entity is narrower.
'Being' in its full latitude supposits for substrates in relation to entity, as 'white' does in relation to whiteness.
Where being is, entity is, but entity is not predicated of everything of which being is predicated.
